..
Issued at 303 AM CDT Thu Sep 17 2026

Ridging and warm air pushed a little further north Wednesday 
afternoon which was a bit further than anticipated, but not 
surprising. This is part of a expansive high pressure across the SE 
CONUS building a bit northwestward. The two primary effects of this 
are warming temperatures and clearing skies through the overnight. 
This has also pushed the flow of upper level shortwaves NW keeping 
rain chance mostly across NE and IA, although there is a chance for 
a stray shower across far NW MO during the early morning hours. What 
is more likely though is some fog development as slowly departing 
rains on Wednesday have left much of far northern MO saturated and 
radiational cooling has fairly quickly shrunk dew point depressions 
creating a favorable environment for fog. The nighttime microphysics 
channel of GOES EAST shows low clouds and for extending from Holt 
County MO northeast through Schuyler County. Areas of dense fog 
(Visibility < 1/4) mile are possible yield a dense fog advisory for 
the NW corner with possible expansion SE depending on how fog 
advects from weather to the north. It is unlikely dense fog will 
extend much past the US-36 corridor.

Fog dissipates after sunrise with southerly flow once again 
dominating. The good news is that surface level southerly flow is 
rather meager which results in weaker warm air advection. This keeps 
the general pattern of more pleasant conditions across the north of 
the area and much hotter to the south; however, the gradient become 
much less stark. Highs north of I-70 range from the 80s to the low 
90s with areas south of I-70 from the 90s to near 100F. Heat index 
values crest 100F along and south of the MO River peaking at 105-107 
across central and SW MO.

This warming trend continues into Friday as the high ever so slowly 
build northward. However, on the opposite side of the country, a low 
digs from the Pacific NW which has a little more success showing its 
way south and eastward. This puts the exit region of this upper low 
over the Rockies creating a channel for lee trough development. This 
tries to piece together showers and storms Friday morning across NE 
and IA, but becomes more successful during the afternoon and evening 
as low level lee cyclogenesis develops across eastern CO and western 
KS. Model guidance remains somewhat uncertain as to the location of 
where this cyclogenesis will manifest itself, but consensus places it 
in the eastern CO foothills to the NE Sand Hills. As such, this 
looks to compress the pressure gradient across the central CONUS as 
the system begins intruding upon the high to the SE. As it does so, 
accelerated warm air and moisture advection lift temperatures. 
Strangely, this will be on display overnight Friday into Saturday as 
most areas will see lows in the low to mid 70s. The nocturnal LLJ 
will also crank up combined with multiple avenues for ascent 
resulting in showers and thunderstorms developing early Saturday 
morning. Ensemble guidance places the most likely chances for 
showers Saturday morning across far NW MO, but it is not implausible 
for rain chances to extend southward toward the I-70 corridor. 

As the Sat AM lee trough moves, it runs into resistance from the 
high to the east. This deflects the system toward the northeast. 
However, additional waves are expected to travel this path thanks in 
part to a synoptic cold front that is expected to approach Saturday 
afternoon. This large scale front also runs into resistance from the 
high creating a channel across KS and NW MO for the waves and 
accompanying rain to follow. This set up sticks around through 
Sunday into early Monday looking fairly similar to what we saw 
Tuesday and Wednesday. This brings the potential for training 
showers and storms along a SW to NE oriented boundary. It remains 
fairly uncertain the exact hazards and impacts as resolution of 
convective variables remains rather course. The air mass behind this 
front is notably cooler than what we currently have, and such a 
transition is unlikely without at least a slim chance for isolated 
robust convection. PWAT values around 2 inches are on the higher 
side of normal creating an environment for heavy downpours. 
Uncertainties will narrow as higher resolution guidance comes into 
range.

The good news is that behind the cold front, temperatures dip back 
into the 70s and 80s. The upper level high is slowly beat into 
submission creating more zonal flow across the interior CONUS. This 
brings more transitive flow of system through the continent which 
looks to keep the extended pattern active with multiple chances 
for rain through the next week.
